rows.tested_claim: Direct critical response to Languages of Class.
rows.outcome: Confirmed through Fontes’s focused scholarly reconstruction and quotations of the 1987 review, independently corroborated by Palmer (1993), p. 143. Original 1987 review body unavailable; the society index confirms issue/pages but not argument.

rows.author: John Foster
rows.tested_claim: The declassing of language neglects social practice and consciousness.
rows.outcome: Kirk’s own 1987 discussion, p. 4/n6, explicitly attributes this objection to Foster, with p. 43 locator; p. 47/n143 identifies Foster’s criticism of the idealist thrust. This confirms a particular materialist criticism without treating it as opposition to language study itself.
rows.body_extent: Fresh NLR accessible opening only; current paywall prevents fresh full-body reading. The prior full-reading record remains unchanged. Fresh Kirk pp. 2–7 and 46–47 supply explicit named mediation.
rows.identity_limit: John Foster has no individual node; John Bellamy Foster is a different person.
rows.representation: Existing mixed edge_1159 stays; no invented individual endpoint.

rows.author: Neville Kirk
rows.tested_claim: Class-based reading defends material constraints against an overly autonomous language and politics.
rows.outcome: Confirmed in Kirk’s stated program and conclusion. He simultaneously endorses opposition to economic reductionism, contextual complexity and attention to language/politics. Not a simple rejection of linguistic investigation.
rows.body_extent: Fresh selected primary pp. 2–7 and 46–47, including notes 6–8 and 143. Middle body not freshly reread in full. Earlier recorded reading scope retained (selected pp. 2–5 and 44–47, plus the earlier pp. 6–7 and 14–17); no whole-article read claimed.
rows.identity_limit: Neville Kirk has no individual node; Sylvia Van Kirk is a different person.
rows.representation: Mixed edge_1159 preserved. Note 8’s statement that Jones does not directly address Dorothy concerns the reverse direction and does not disprove her later critique.

rows.author: Neville Kirk
rows.tested_claim: The later materialist argument supplies a separate direct response.
rows.outcome: Bibliographic existence confirmed independently by Astra. This article’s particular argument, reply targets and differences from the 1987 critique remain unverified here; do not infer them from the title or transfer 1987 claims.

rows.author: Ellen Meiksins Wood
rows.tested_claim: Historical language does not warrant an autonomous politics detached from class conditions.
rows.outcome: Confirmed in selected chapter 7 text. Wood expressly distinguishes Jones’s substantial historical work from other abstract theorists, and targets the conclusions drawn from his evidence. His rejection of mechanical correspondence need not entail general non-correspondence. A separate 1995 passage explains inherited radicalism’s transformation under capitalist relations.
rows.body_extent: Fresh pp. 102–107 in third-party transcription of the revised 1998 edition, with front matter checked. Not facsimile-collated; no assertion of unchanged text since 1986. Separate official publisher translation of Democracy against Capitalism (1995), German edition 2010, pp. 79–80/n31 and front matter read. Neither whole book read.

rows.author: Bryan D. Palmer
rows.tested_claim: Descent into Discourse supplies materialist criticism of Jones.
rows.outcome: The 1990 book’s existence and topic are confirmed, but its detailed treatment is not freshly read. A new arrow uses Palmer’s own independently read 1993 article, pp. 143–146, rather than silently substituting it as proof of the 1990 book’s exact claims.
rows.body_extent: 1990 book body unread; fresh primary 1993 article pp. 143–146 and 154.

rows.author: James Epstein
rows.tested_claim: Jones’s formal public language omits symbolic action, movement culture and contested meanings.
rows.outcome: Confirmed. Epstein praises the reinterpretation and the reality of language, then argues that ritual, collective solidarity and conflict over public terms cannot be reduced to formal ideology. He retains the importance of inherited traditions while making their meanings contested.
rows.body_extent: Fresh primary journal PDF pp. 199–201 and 207–208. Other pages not freshly reread in full; prior full-reading record preserved.
rows.identity_limit: No James Epstein individual node; no new biography or field substitution.

rows.author: James Epstein
rows.tested_claim: Radical Expression elaborates the same criticism through ritual and symbolism.
rows.outcome: Book metadata confirmed by Astra. Its specific argument and relation to the 1986 essay remain unverified here; no assertion that it simply reprints that essay or repeats all its criticisms.

rows.author: Paul A. Pickering
rows.tested_claim: Symbolic/nonverbal Chartist communication challenges Jones’s restricted corpus.
rows.outcome: Kirk p. 5/n7 explicitly places Pickering among the critics whose general lines he follows in defending Chartism’s social/class character. Eley/Nield p. 7/n19 lists it among substantive contributions postdating Jones’s intervention and carrying discussion beyond his essay. These confirm a relevant response, but no detailed reconstruction of Pickering’s individual examples or conclusions is claimed from his title alone.
rows.body_extent: Publisher metadata freshly checked; original article body not retrieved. Fresh named-reader passages in Kirk and Eley/Nield read.

rows.author: Robert Gray
rows.tested_claim: Jones treats linguistic theory as a settled method and language too formally.
rows.outcome: Kirk p. 4/n6 explicitly quotes Gray p. 367 on post-structuralist language analysis as a field of debate, and attributes the criticism of narrow formal words rather than constructed social meaning to Gray and Foster. This supports a bounded methodological objection, not blanket hostility to language.
rows.body_extent: Gray original body unread; fresh Kirk p. 4/n6 and Eley/Nield pp. 6–8/n19 read.
rows.identity_limit: Robert (Robbie) Gray has no individual node; Deborah Gray White is a different person.

dorothy_specific_subclaims.limit: Dorothy is credited with insisting on other verbal/nonverbal communication and wider archival sources. Rich oral/visual culture is also explicitly Epstein’s argument; do not assign every example to Dorothy.

dorothy_specific_subclaims.claim: Constitutional idiom does not negate class
dorothy_specific_subclaims.limit: Fontes explicitly presents Dorothy’s rejection of the rigid dichotomy between political and social/class movement. The exact constitutional-idiom phrasing is not independently verified from her original.

global_limits: The 1982 Language of Chartism is only a partial earlier version of the 1983 Rethinking Chartism; not an unchanged reprint. Dorothy 1984, review 1987, Outsiders 1993 and Dignity of Chartism 2015 remain distinct manifestations. The original 1987 review and later collection bodies remain unread. No general consensus, uniform two-flank camp, or complete reading of all books is claimed.
